candidate.title: Formal representation and constraint-aware generation of selected Asante Kente weaving structures
candidate.workingTitle: Formal Representation and Constraint-Aware Generation of Selected Asante Kente Weaving Structures
candidate.summary: Can selected Asante Kente design structures be represented computationally and generated with explicit constraints linking motif, weave structure and the operations of a specified indigenous loom?
candidate.shortDescription: A Ghana-grounded computational study of Kente-specific structural grammar, loom-operation representation, constraint-aware generation and physical/expert validation.
candidate.ghanaianRelevance: Directly grounded in Ghanaian textile practice. The scope must stay on selected structures rather than all Kente traditions.
candidate.technicalContribution: A machine-readable representation linking selected Asante Kente motifs, weave/interlacement structure and loom-operation sequence; explicit constraints for a bounded loom context; and a generation/validation method. The contribution must go beyond producing a visual pattern or a generic weave draft. It must distinguish traditional Bonwire narrow-strip practice from modified two-heddle/countershaft or multi-shaft handloom systems documented in related Ghanaian studies.

feasibility.rationale: This is a planning assessment. Feasibility depends on reliable weave-structure information and a testable definition of loom compatibility.

candidate.dataRequirements: Selected Asante Kente structures and motifs; source-checked structural descriptions and point-paper/draft examples; documented warp/weft, heddling, shaft, lifting/treadling and tie-up information for the specified loom; and practitioner input for validation. Vigbedor et al. (2024) documents WeavePoint 7.2 use for weave, draft, lifting/stepping order and tie-up with test weaving on a modified indigenous two-heddle loom. Vigbedor et al. (2026) reports physical fabric production and artisan evaluation on a modified four-post countershaft handloom using four-to-six shaft configurations, including master weavers from Bonwire and Agortime-Kpetoe. Neither paper by itself establishes a Kente-specific grammar or proves equivalence to the traditional Bonwire narrow-strip loom. Data availability in these papers is by reasonable request; access is not guaranteed.
candidate.evaluationDesign: Define one target loom context and a bounded set of Kente structures. Compare unconstrained or generic generation with a formal Kente-specific representation and constraint-aware generation. Evaluate representation completeness, structural validity, constraint satisfaction, motif/structure fidelity, diversity, and completeness/consistency of loom-operation outputs (e.g. draft, heddling, lifting/treadling and tie-up as applicable to the selected loom). Obtain expert review and, if feasible, physically weave a small number of outputs on the specified target loom. Physical results from a modified countershaft or multi-shaft loom must not be reported as validation on a traditional narrow-strip loom.
majorRisks: The target loom and the meaning of loom compatibility are still not fixed. A traditional Bonwire narrow-strip loom, a modified indigenous two-heddle loom and a four-to-six-shaft countershaft handloom are not interchangeable contexts.

Recent Ghanaian studies already demonstrate WeavePoint-based drafts, lifting/stepping plans, tie-up and physical test weaving; novelty cannot be claimed merely for converting an image into a weave draft.
The 2026 countershaft study includes artisans from Bonwire and Agortime-Kpetoe, but its modified four-post, four-to-six-shaft setup must not be assumed to document traditional narrow-strip operation.
A generic textile grammar may fail to capture the relationship between selected Asante Kente motifs, weave structure and the specified loom operations.
Practitioner access, loom access and physical validation may be difficult to secure within the MPhil timeline.
If reliable operation data cannot be obtained, the thesis must narrow its claim to formal structural validity rather than production-ready loom compatibility.
openDecisions: Which bounded Asante Kente pattern structures and motif families will be represented?
What exact target loom is in scope: traditional Bonwire narrow-strip loom, a specified modified indigenous two-heddle loom, or another explicitly documented setup?
Which loom-operation variables are required for the selected loom (e.g. warp/weft, heddling, shaft assignment, lifting/treadling, tie-up and pick sequence)?
How will the thesis distinguish and validate traditional narrow-strip practice against the modified two-heddle and four-to-six-shaft countershaft systems described in Vigbedor et al.?
Can the relevant loom specifications, WeavePoint/draft examples and practitioner access be obtained early enough to support physical or expert validation?

nodes.title: Visual Kente-like patterns do not necessarily encode valid weaving structure or loom operations
nodes.summary: A convincing pattern image may omit the interlacement and operation sequence needed to reproduce it on a specified indigenous loom.
nodes.detail: The research has moved beyond asking whether AI can draw Kente-like patterns. Recent Ghanaian weaving studies demonstrate that indigenous loom structures can be represented through weave drafts, heddling/lifting plans, tie-up information and physical test weaving. The technical research opportunity is therefore to formalise a Kente-specific relationship between selected motifs, interlacement structure and the operations of one specified loom, then generate and validate patterns against those constraints. The modified two-heddle and countershaft systems in the recent studies must not be assumed equivalent to the traditional Bonwire narrow-strip loom.
assumptions: A bounded set of structures is sufficient for an MPhil contribution.
A formal representation can capture the constraints needed for the chosen loom and pattern class.
Visual similarity is not evidence of weaveability.
risks: The research may become textile documentation rather than IT unless the representation, constraint model, generator, and evaluation are technically central.
Practitioner knowledge may be needed to validate the rules.

nodes.title: How can selected Asante Kente structures be represented and generated with constraints linking motif, weave structure and specified loom operations?
nodes.summary: How can a bounded Kente-specific structural grammar support constraint-aware generation and validation for one explicitly defined loom context?
nodes.detail: The central question is how to encode selected Asante Kente motifs and weave structures in a machine-readable representation that also captures the operation sequence required by a specified loom. The recent literature shows that digital drafts and physical weaving tests already exist for modified indigenous loom systems. The thesis must identify what is specific to the selected Kente structures and target loom, and must not claim that a generic draft or a modified countershaft sample proves compatibility with a traditional narrow-strip loom.

nodes.title: Why this is a computing problem
nodes.summary: The contribution has to be a representation, a constraint model, and an evaluation, not only a description of Kente.
nodes.detail: This direction fits MPhil IT when its main contribution is a formal representation, a computational constraint model, a generation/repair method, and reproducible evaluation. The cultural context grounds the problem but is not a substitute for the computing contribution.

nodes.title: Grounded in Asante weaving practice
nodes.summary: Grounded in Asante weaving practice
nodes.detail: The direction is grounded in Ghanaian textile practice. That relevance does not by itself make the work a computing contribution, and it does not license claims about all Kente traditions.

nodes.title: A representation and a constraint check
nodes.summary: A representation and a constraint check
nodes.detail: The technical object can be modelled in layers: visible design/motif arrangement; underlying weave structure; loom-specific execution constraints; and validation of the mapping between them. A narrow-loom practice and broadloom translation must not be treated as interchangeable. Candidate representation elements discussed include warp/weft and supplementary-weft structure, point-paper grids, motif-to-draft mappings, drafts, heddling, shafts, and tie-up. The final representation should include only the elements that can be documented and validated.

nodes.title: What would count as a contribution
nodes.summary: What would count as a contribution
nodes.detail: A defensible contribution could comprise (1) a machine-readable representation for a bounded set of Kente structures, (2) explicit structural/loom constraints, (3) a generator that rejects or repairs invalid candidates, and (4) an evaluation protocol that distinguishes visual appearance from structural validity and execution feasibility.

nodes.title: Structured representation of selected motifs
nodes.summary: Structured representation of selected motifs
nodes.detail: A small, documented, machine-readable corpus of selected motifs and associated weave structures. It should record provenance and scope; it is not intended as a complete catalogue of Kente. The literature discussion specifically referenced Ahwepan, Topreko, Faprenu, and Asasia as named structures documented by Badoe & Opoku-Asare (2014); verify the source and the scope before selecting any of them.

nodes.title: Formal constraint model
nodes.summary: Formal constraint model
nodes.detail: A formal set of structural and loom-specific constraints that can be tested automatically. Each rule should be traceable to documentation or practitioner validation.

nodes.title: Generation method
nodes.summary: Generation method
nodes.detail: A computational method that generates candidate patterns under the selected representation and constraints, with explicit handling of invalid outputs (rejection, repair, or constrained search).

nodes.title: Machine-checkable validation
nodes.summary: Machine-checkable validation
nodes.detail: A reproducible validator reporting rule violations, constraint satisfaction, structural validity, diversity, and instruction completeness. The validator must not equate pixel similarity with successful weaving.

nodes.title: External check, only if feasible
nodes.summary: External check, only if feasible
nodes.detail: If access and time permit, experienced weavers assess whether the representation and instructions correspond to the selected practice; a small physical weave test is optional and must not be promised before access is confirmed.
risks: Do not make physical production validation a dependency unless loom and practitioner access are secured early.

nodes.title: Generation methods may optimise appearance
nodes.summary: Generation methods may optimise appearance
nodes.detail: The project discussions identified FabricGen/WeavingLLM, shape-grammar work, and other computational textile systems as important prior-art leads. One discussion described FabricGen/WeavingLLM as involving 1,142 drafts. These details are discovery notes only: the exact bibliographic records, system capabilities, and whether they encode physical loom constraints must be checked in the full texts. Generic textile generation is therefore not a safe novelty claim.

nodes.title: Visual plausibility may be produced without a specific weaving process
nodes.summary: Visual plausibility may be produced without a specific weaving process
nodes.detail: A possible gap is the distance between generating a visually plausible textile design and representing constraints that make a pattern valid for a specified weaving process. The existence and extent of this gap are unconfirmed until FabricGen/WeavingLLM, shape-grammar work, and other relevant systems are inspected for their representations, constraints, and validation methods.
assumptions: The selected prior systems may optimise visual or design-level output without modelling the selected loom process; this must be checked, not assumed.
validationRequirements: Extract each system’s input/output representation, weaving assumptions, structural constraints, and validation procedure.

nodes.title: Structural patterns are documented for design education
nodes.summary: Structural patterns are documented for design education
nodes.detail: The project discussions referenced Badoe (2005), Badoe and Opoku-Asare, and other Ghanaian textile/Kente documentation as cultural and structural background. The exact bibliographic records and the extent to which these sources formalise motifs, weave structures, or loom execution remain to be verified. The discussion identified Badoe & Opoku-Asare (2014) as describing Ahwepan, Topreko, Faprenu, Asasia, motif/point-paper grids, drafts, heddling, shafts, tie-up, and composition rules, including student motif-to-draft-to-broadloom examples. This is a project literature note and needs direct source verification.

nodes.title: General textile models may not capture Asante Kente conventions
nodes.summary: General textile models may not capture Asante Kente conventions
nodes.detail: A possible contribution is a machine-readable representation specific to a bounded set of Asante Kente structures, rather than applying a generic textile representation unchanged. This is a candidate gap, not an established absence: existing textile grammars, design tools, and Kente documentation must be compared first. The potential technical distinction is not merely digitising motifs: it is preserving the relationship between motif, weave draft, and the specific loom execution process.
risks: Do not model all Kente traditions. Select a bounded set of structures.
validationRequirements: Determine whether existing Kente documentation already provides a formal representation suitable for computation.

nodes.title: Existing loom-design workflows can represent drafts and operation plans, so image-to-draft alone is not novel
nodes.summary: Tools and papers may stop at the drawing
nodes.detail: Vigbedor et al. (2024) report using WeavePoint 7.2 to develop the weave, draft, lifting/stepping order and tie-up, followed by test weaving on an indigenous two-heddle loom modified with a countershaft shedding mechanism. This establishes a Ghanaian precedent for connecting digital weave plans to physical weaving. It does not establish a Kente-specific computational grammar or the operation rules of the traditional Bonwire narrow-strip loom. The thesis contribution must be more precise than simply translating an image into a draft.

nodes.title: A Kente-specific mapping from motif and weave structure to the target loom operation sequence remains to be established
nodes.summary: A digital pattern may not be an executable weaving specification
nodes.detail: The gap should not be framed as a general absence of digital weaving plans: WeavePoint-based weave/draft/lifting/tie-up information and physical test weaving are already documented in Ghanaian indigenous loom research. The narrower hypothesis is whether selected Asante Kente structures can be represented in a formal grammar that preserves motif-to-interlacement relationships and maps them to complete, valid operations for one specified loom context. This requires full-text comparison and technical/practitioner validation; it is not yet an established absence.
risks: If loom specifications or knowledgeable reviewers are not available, narrow the claim to structurally constrained pattern generation.

nodes.title: Kente-specific structural grammar and loom-operation representation
nodes.summary: How should selected Kente motifs, interlacement structures and loom operations be encoded together?
nodes.detail: This area captures the main technical contribution after reviewing Ghanaian loom-engineering work. It distinguishes the design layer, weave/interlacement layer and loom-operation layer, and asks how they can be linked in a formal representation for one bounded Kente and loom scope.

nodes.title: Ghanaian loom research already links digital drafts to physical test weaving
nodes.summary: A 2024 study reports WeavePoint 7.2 drafts, lifting/stepping order, tie-up and test weaving on a modified indigenous two-heddle loom.
nodes.detail: Vigbedor, Akrofi, Bruce-Amartey Jnr. and Howard describe integrating a countershaft shedding mechanism into an indigenous two-heddle loom. The paper reports use of WeavePoint 7.2 to create the weave, draft, lifting/stepping order and tie-up, followed by physical test weaving. This is a relevant methodological and technical precedent. It is not evidence that the same operation plan applies unchanged to a traditional Bonwire narrow-strip loom, nor that the work provides a formal Kente-specific computational grammar.

nodes.title: Recent Ghanaian research includes multi-shaft indigenous handloom trials and artisan evaluation
nodes.summary: A 2026 study reports fabric production and physical/mechanical evaluation on a modified four-post countershaft handloom with four-to-six shaft configurations.
nodes.detail: Vigbedor, Akrofi, Nyante, Asinyo and Frimpong report a modified indigenous four-post handloom with a countershaft shedding system. The study produced plain derivatives, twills, diamonds and satin structures across four-to-six shaft configurations; it combined tensile and drape assessments with artisan evaluation involving master weavers from Bonwire and Agortime-Kpetoe. This supports the feasibility of physical and practitioner validation in Ghanaian weaving research. However, the modified multi-shaft setup is not automatically equivalent to traditional Bonwire narrow-strip practice.

nodes.title: A Kente-specific formal mapping from motif grammar to target loom operations still needs to be demonstrated
nodes.summary: The potential contribution is the formal relationship between selected Asante Kente design structures, interlacement and a specified loom operation sequence.
nodes.detail: The checked Ghanaian loom studies demonstrate digital draft/operation plans and physical validation on modified indigenous looms. They do not, in the checked abstracts, establish a machine-readable grammar for selected Asante Kente motifs that maps to validated operations on the traditional Bonwire narrow-strip loom. This is a bounded hypothesis, not a claim that no such work exists. Full-text analysis of Kente structural documentation, the two Vigbedor studies and other textile-generation systems is required before asserting novelty.

nodes.title: Build a formal design–weave–operation representation for a bounded set of Asante Kente structures
nodes.summary: Represent selected motifs, weave structure and target-loom operation sequence in one constraint-checkable model.
nodes.detail: A suitable topic would define a small Kente pattern class and one loom context, encode the design and interlacement relationships, and represent the required operation sequence. Generation should be constrained by this representation, with machine-checkable validation and expert/physical validation where feasible. The study should not expand to every Kente tradition or every indigenous loom.

nodes.title: How can selected Asante Kente motifs, weave structures and loom operations be represented in a machine-readable grammar?
nodes.summary: What representation preserves the relationships between motif arrangement, interlacement structure and the operation sequence for the specified loom?
nodes.detail: The answer should define the model entities and relationships, identify which structural and operational constraints are machine-checkable, and state which knowledge must be supplied or validated by practitioners.
validationRequirements: Specify the target loom and bounded Kente structure class.
Represent the design, weave/interlacement and loom-operation layers separately but link them explicitly.
Validate encoded rules against source-checked drafts and knowledgeable practitioners.

nodes.title: Can generated Kente patterns be translated into complete and physically valid loom instructions?
nodes.summary: To what extent do generated outputs satisfy structural constraints and produce complete operation plans that can be checked by experts or physically woven on the specified loom?
nodes.detail: The evaluation should distinguish machine-checkable constraint satisfaction from expert judgement and physical weaving outcomes. A sample woven on a modified countershaft loom must not be presented as proof of compatibility with a different traditional narrow-strip loom.
validationRequirements: Report structural validity and constraint satisfaction separately from visual similarity.
Check draft, heddling, lifting/treadling and tie-up completeness as applicable to the chosen loom.
Obtain practitioner assessment and, if feasible, physical weaving on the actual target loom.

evidenceLinks.claim: Project discussions identify Tang et al. (2026), described as FabricGen/WeavingLLM, as a recent computational textile-generation lead; one discussion noted 1,142 drafts.
evidenceLinks.limitation: The exact paper and the 1,142-draft detail are not verified here. It is not established whether the system models a specific physical weaving process or loom-level constraints.
evidenceLinks.notes: Treat as a high-priority full-text verification task, not as confirmed evidence for the gap.

evidenceLinks.claim: Project notes describe Wang et al. (2026) as shape-grammar work that might bear on pattern structure.
evidenceLinks.limitation: It is not yet known whether the work addresses textile structure.
evidenceLinks.notes: Bibliographic record and the paper's actual findings still need to be checked.

evidenceLinks.claim: Badoe (2005) is cited in the project notes as an analytical study of Asante Kente structural patterns.
evidenceLinks.limitation: The notes do not establish a machine-readable specification or a generation algorithm.
evidenceLinks.notes: Bibliographic record and the paper's actual findings still need to be checked.

evidenceLinks.claim: Project notes identify Badoe & Opoku-Asare (2014) as documenting Asante Kente structures including Ahwepan, Topreko, Faprenu, and Asasia, with motif/point-paper and draft-related instructional material.
evidenceLinks.limitation: The full text and bibliographic record have not been checked here. Notes mention broadloom examples; they do not establish Bonwire narrow-strip-loom execution rules.
evidenceLinks.notes: Priority full-text review. Extract the structures, draft notation, heddling, shafts, tie-up, and any limits on translating instructional examples to a traditional narrow-strip loom.

evidenceLinks.claim: Sawyerr et al. (2026) is a lead on Ghanaian textile AI.
evidenceLinks.limitation: Relevance to weave structure, rather than visual generation, is unverified.
evidenceLinks.notes: Bibliographic record and the paper's actual findings still need to be checked.

evidenceLinks.claim: Project discussions describe an Ikat co-design study in which digital designs reportedly required interpretation or modification by weavers and physical validation.
evidenceLinks.limitation: Exact title, study protocol, sample, and findings are unverified. The observation cannot be generalised to Kente or all textile-generation systems.
evidenceLinks.notes: Extract how designers/weavers evaluated digital outputs and whether physical weaving was actually performed.

evidenceLinks.claim: weaveDraft is recorded as a software tool that may expose weave information.
evidenceLinks.limitation: No research paper has been identified, and its loom assumptions are unknown.
evidenceLinks.notes: Bibliographic record and the paper's actual findings still need to be checked.

evidenceLinks.claim: The article reports WeavePoint 7.2 use to create weave, draft, lifting/stepping order and tie-up, followed by test weaving on a modified indigenous two-heddle loom.
evidenceLinks.limitation: This is a modified two-heddle/countershaft setup and not a direct specification for traditional Bonwire narrow-strip operation or a Kente-specific grammar.

evidenceLinks.claim: The article reports a modified indigenous four-post countershaft handloom with four-to-six shaft configurations, physical fabric testing and artisan evaluation involving master weavers from Bonwire and Agortime-Kpetoe.
evidenceLinks.limitation: The modified multi-shaft setup is not automatically equivalent to a traditional Bonwire narrow-strip loom; the study does not establish a Kente-specific computational representation.

evidenceLinks.claim: This study demonstrates that digital weave/draft/lifting/tie-up plans and physical test weaving have already been used in Ghanaian indigenous loom research.
evidenceLinks.limitation: It concerns loom modification and test weaving, not the proposed Kente-specific grammar; it therefore narrows the novelty claim rather than proving the proposed gap.

evidenceLinks.claim: This study demonstrates physical fabric production and practitioner evaluation on a modified indigenous handloom involving Bonwire and Agortime-Kpetoe master weavers.
evidenceLinks.limitation: Its modified four-to-six-shaft countershaft setup is not evidence of traditional narrow-strip loom compatibility or a machine-readable Kente grammar.
